name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MATCH_Q01 - Scientists and their early photosynthesis experiments

questiontext.text:
Match the scientists in List I with their respective contributions to the study of photosynthesis in List II:

List I (Scientist)List II (Contribution)
(A) Joseph Priestley(i) Provided evidence for glucose production stored as starch in chloroplasts
(B) Jan Ingenhousz(ii) Described the first action spectrum using Cladophora and aerobic bacteria
(C) Julius von Sachs(iii) Revealed the essential role of air in the growth of green plants using a bell jar
(D) T.W. Engelmann(iv) Showed that sunlight is essential and only green parts release oxygen bubbles

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Early experiments progressively established the roles of air, sunlight, green plant parts (chloroplasts), and specific wavelengths of light in photosynthesis.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Joseph Priestley (1770) used a bell jar with a burning candle, a mouse, and a mint plant to show that plants restore to the air whatever breathing animals and burning candles remove.
Jan Ingenhousz used an aquatic plant in dark and sunlight to demonstrate that sunlight is essential and that only green parts release oxygen bubbles.
Julius von Sachs (1854) showed that green parts make glucose, usually stored as starch, and that chlorophyll is located in chloroplasts.
T.W. Engelmann split light with a prism onto Cladophora in a suspension of aerobic bacteria, observing bacterial accumulation in the blue and red regions and thus describing the first action spectrum.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Joseph Priestley with the bell jar experiment on air restoration, Jan Ingenhousz with sunlight and oxygen release by green parts, Julius von Sachs with glucose/starch in chloroplasts, and T.W. Engelmann with the first action spectrum using Cladophora.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MATCH_Q02 - Leaf pigments and their chromatogram colours

questiontext.text:
Match the leaf pigments in List I with their characteristic colours in a paper chromatogram and roles in List II:

List I (Pigment)List II (Chromatogram Colour & Role)
(A) Chlorophyll a(i) Yellow in chromatogram; accessory pigment
(B) Chlorophyll b(ii) Yellow to yellow-orange in chromatogram; accessory pigment
(C) Xanthophylls(iii) Bright or blue-green in chromatogram; chief photosynthetic pigment
(D) Carotenoids(iv) Yellow-green in chromatogram; accessory pigment

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chromatographic separation of leaf pigments reveals four distinct pigments that absorb light at specific wavelengths to drive photosynthesis.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Chlorophyll a appears bright or blue-green in the chromatogram and serves as the chief pigment associated with photosynthesis.
Chlorophyll b appears yellow-green in the chromatogram and acts as an accessory pigment.
Xanthophylls appear yellow in the chromatogram and act as accessory pigments.
Carotenoids appear yellow to yellow-orange in the chromatogram and act as accessory pigments that widen the absorbed wavelength range and protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs chlorophyll a with bright or blue-green (chief pigment), chlorophyll b with yellow-green, xanthophylls with yellow, and carotenoids with yellow to yellow-orange.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MATCH_Q03 - Photosystems and light reaction complexes

questiontext.text:
Match the light-reaction components in List I with their characteristic features or locations in List II:

List I (Component)List II (Feature / Location)
(A) PS I reaction centre(i) Physically located on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane with PS II
(B) PS II reaction centre(ii) Located on the stroma side of the thylakoid membrane
(C) Water-splitting complex(iii) Chlorophyll a molecule with absorption peak at \(700\ \text{nm}\) (P700)
(D) NADP reductase enzyme(iv) Chlorophyll a molecule with absorption maxima at \(680\ \text{nm}\) (P680)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The photochemical phase of photosynthesis involves two discrete photosystems (PS I and PS II) and membrane-bound complexes arranged asymmetrically across the thylakoid membrane.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
The PS I reaction centre is a single chlorophyll a molecule with an absorption peak at \(700\ \text{nm}\), termed P700.
The PS II reaction centre is a single chlorophyll a molecule with an absorption maximum at \(680\ \text{nm}\), termed P680.
The water-splitting complex is associated with PS II and is physically located on the inner (lumen) side of the thylakoid membrane, releasing protons and \(\mathrm{O_2}\) into the lumen.
The NADP reductase enzyme is located on the stroma side of the thylakoid membrane, where it uses electrons from PS I and protons from the stroma to reduce \(\mathrm{NADP^+}\) to \(\mathrm{NADPH + H^+}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs PS I reaction centre with P700 (\(700\ \text{nm}\)), PS II reaction centre with P680 (\(680\ \text{nm}\)), water-splitting complex with the inner side of the thylakoid membrane, and NADP reductase with the stroma side.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MATCH_Q04 - Chemiosmotic hypothesis components in chloroplasts

questiontext.text:
Match the chemiosmotic components in List I with their exact functions or properties in chloroplasts in List II:

List I (Component)List II (Function / Property)
(A) Thylakoid lumen(i) Protrudes on the outer stromal surface; undergoes conformational change to synthesise ATP
(B) \(\mathrm{CF_0}\)(ii) Removes a proton from the stroma and releases it into the lumen during electron transfer
(C) \(\mathrm{CF_1}\)(iii) Site of proton accumulation causing a measurable decrease in pH
(D) H-carrier(iv) Embedded in the thylakoid membrane; forms a transmembrane channel for facilitated proton diffusion

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chemiosmotic ATP synthesis in chloroplasts depends on establishing a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane and breaking it down through ATP synthase.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Protons accumulate inside the thylakoid lumen, creating a proton gradient and a measurable decrease in luminal pH.
The \(\mathrm{CF_0}\) portion of ATP synthase is embedded in the thylakoid membrane and forms a transmembrane channel that carries out facilitated diffusion of protons back to the stroma.
The \(\mathrm{CF_1}\) portion protrudes on the outer surface of the thylakoid membrane facing the stroma; breakdown of the proton gradient induces a conformational change in \(\mathrm{CF_1}\) to synthesise ATP.
An H-carrier receives an electron from the primary acceptor on the outer side, picks up a proton from the stroma, and releases that proton into the lumen when passing the electron to an inner electron carrier.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs the thylakoid lumen with proton accumulation and decreased pH, \(\mathrm{CF_0}\) with the transmembrane channel, \(\mathrm{CF_1}\) with the stromal ATP-synthesising subunit, and the H-carrier with proton translocation from stroma to lumen.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MATCH_Q05 - Calvin cycle stages and energy stoichiometry

questiontext.text:
Match the Calvin cycle stages and quantities in List I with their corresponding biochemical events or energy requirements in List II:

List I (Stage / Quantity)List II (Event / Requirement)
(A) Carboxylation(i) Net input of \(18\text{ ATP}\) and \(12\text{ NADPH}\) to form one glucose molecule
(B) Reduction(ii) Utilisation of \(1\text{ ATP}\) per \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) fixed to reform RuBP
(C) Regeneration(iii) Fixation of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) into two molecules of 3-PGA catalysed by RuBisCO
(D) 6 turns of Calvin cycle(iv) Utilisation of \(2\text{ ATP}\) and \(2\text{ NADPH}\) per \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) fixed

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Calvin cycle operates in three sequential stages—carboxylation, reduction, and regeneration—to fix \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) into carbohydrate while regenerating the primary acceptor RuBP.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Carboxylation is the fixation of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) onto RuBP, catalysed by RuBisCO, yielding two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA).
Reduction involves a series of reactions that consume \(2\text{ ATP}\) for phosphorylation and \(2\text{ NADPH}\) for reduction per \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) molecule fixed.
Regeneration of RuBP requires \(1\text{ ATP}\) for phosphorylation per \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) fixed so the cycle can continue uninterrupted.
Six turns of the cycle fix \(6\ \mathrm{CO_2}\) molecules to produce one molecule of glucose, requiring \(6 \times 3 = 18\text{ ATP}\) and \(6 \times 2 = 12\text{ NADPH}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs carboxylation with RuBisCO-catalysed formation of 3-PGA, reduction with \(2\text{ ATP}\) and \(2\text{ NADPH}\) per \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), regeneration with \(1\text{ ATP}\) per \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), and 6 turns with \(18\text{ ATP}\) and \(12\text{ NADPH}\) per glucose.

questiontext.text:
Match the photophosphorylation features in List I with their correct descriptions in List II:

List I (Feature)List II (Description)
(A) Non-cyclic photophosphorylation(i) Only ATP is synthesised; no \(\mathrm{NADPH + H^+}\) is formed
(B) Cyclic photophosphorylation(ii) Both ATP and \(\mathrm{NADPH + H^+}\) are synthesised
(C) Products of non-cyclic flow(iii) Involves only PS I; occurs when only wavelengths beyond \(680\ \text{nm}\) are available
(D) Products of cyclic flow(iv) Involves PS II and PS I working in series via the Z-scheme

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Photophosphorylation is the light-driven synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate, occurring via either non-cyclic or cyclic electron flow.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Non-cyclic photophosphorylation occurs when PS II and PS I work in series connected through the electron transport chain (Z-scheme).
Cyclic photophosphorylation occurs when only PS I is functional (such as in stroma lamellae or when only light beyond \(680\ \text{nm}\) is available).
Non-cyclic electron flow synthesises both ATP and \(\mathrm{NADPH + H^+}\).
Cyclic electron flow cycles electrons back to PS I and synthesises only ATP without producing \(\mathrm{NADPH + H^+}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs non-cyclic photophosphorylation with PS II and PS I in series, cyclic photophosphorylation with PS I only beyond \(680\ \text{nm}\), products of non-cyclic flow with both ATP and \(\mathrm{NADPH + H^+}\), and products of cyclic flow with ATP only.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MATCH_Q07 - C4 pathway cell types, enzymes, and anatomy

questiontext.text:
Match the \(\mathrm{C_4}\) pathway terms in List I with their characteristic properties in List II:

List I (Term)List II (Property)
(A) Mesophyll cells(i) 3-carbon primary \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) acceptor in \(\mathrm{C_4}\) plants
(B) Bundle sheath cells(ii) Multi-layered wreath-like arrangement around vascular bundles with thick walls impervious to gases
(C) Phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP)(iii) Contain PEPcase and lack RuBisCO; site of initial \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) fixation into OAA
(D) Kranz anatomy(iv) Rich in RuBisCO and lack PEPcase; site of the Calvin cycle in \(\mathrm{C_4}\) plants

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
\(\mathrm{C_4}\) plants employ the Hatch and Slack pathway, spatially separating initial \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) fixation in mesophyll cells from the Calvin cycle in bundle sheath cells.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Mesophyll cells of \(\mathrm{C_4}\) plants contain PEP carboxylase (PEPcase) and lack RuBisCO, performing the initial fixation of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) into oxaloacetic acid (OAA).
Bundle sheath cells are rich in RuBisCO and lack PEPcase; they carry out the Calvin cycle using \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) released from decarboxylation of \(\mathrm{C_4}\) acids.
Phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP) is the 3-carbon primary \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) acceptor present in mesophyll cells.
Kranz anatomy refers to the wreath-like arrangement of large bundle sheath cells in several layers around vascular bundles, characterised by numerous chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange, and no intercellular spaces.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs mesophyll cells with PEPcase and absence of RuBisCO, bundle sheath cells with RuBisCO and absence of PEPcase, PEP with the 3-carbon primary \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) acceptor, and Kranz anatomy with the wreath-like multi-layered bundle sheath arrangement.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MATCH_Q08 - C3 vs C4 plants and photorespiration products

questiontext.text:
Match the physiological characteristics in List I with their correct values or compounds in List II:

List I (Characteristic)List II (Value / Compound)
(A) Primary \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) fixation product in \(\mathrm{C_3}\) plants(i) \(30\text{--}40^\circ\text{C}\)
(B) Primary \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) fixation product in \(\mathrm{C_4}\) plants(ii) Phosphoglycolate (2-carbon)
(C) Unique oxygenation product in photorespiration(iii) 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-carbon)
(D) Temperature optimum of \(\mathrm{C_4}\) plants(iv) Oxaloacetic acid (4-carbon)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
\(\mathrm{C_3}\) and \(\mathrm{C_4}\) plants differ in their first stable \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) fixation products, temperature optima, and occurrence of photorespiration.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
In \(\mathrm{C_3}\) plants, the first stable product of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) fixation is the 3-carbon organic acid 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA).
In \(\mathrm{C_4}\) plants, the first stable product of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) fixation is the 4-carbon organic acid oxaloacetic acid (OAA).
During photorespiration in \(\mathrm{C_3}\) plants, \(\mathrm{O_2}\) binds to RuBisCO, converting RuBP into one molecule of 3-phosphoglycerate and one molecule of the 2-carbon compound phosphoglycolate.
\(\mathrm{C_4}\) plants are adapted to tropical climates and exhibit a higher temperature optimum of \(30\text{--}40^\circ\text{C}\) compared to \(\mathrm{C_3}\) plants (\(20\text{--}25^\circ\text{C}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs the \(\mathrm{C_3}\) primary fixation product with 3-phosphoglyceric acid, the \(\mathrm{C_4}\) primary fixation product with oxaloacetic acid, the photorespiratory oxygenation product with 2-carbon phosphoglycolate, and the \(\mathrm{C_4}\) temperature optimum with \(30\text{--}40^\circ\text{C}\).

questiontext.text:
Match the external factors and saturation points in List I with their quantitative thresholds or physiological effects in List II:

List I (Factor / Parameter)List II (Threshold / Effect)
(A) Light saturation(i) Closes stomata, reducing \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) availability and causing leaf wilting
(B) \(\mathrm{C_4}\) \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) saturation(ii) Seen only beyond \(450\ \mu\text{L L}^{-1}\)
(C) \(\mathrm{C_3}\) \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) saturation(iii) Occurs at \(10\%\) of full sunlight
(D) Water stress(iv) Occurs at about \(360\ \mu\text{L L}^{-1}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
External factors—light intensity, \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) concentration, temperature, and water availability—govern photosynthetic rates according to their saturation thresholds and physiological impacts.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Light saturation occurs at \(10\%\) of full sunlight, so light is rarely limiting except in shade or dense forests.
\(\mathrm{C_4}\) plants show \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) saturation at about \(360\ \mu\text{L L}^{-1}\).
\(\mathrm{C_3}\) plants respond to higher \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) concentrations, with saturation seen only beyond \(450\ \mu\text{L L}^{-1}\), making current atmospheric \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) limiting for \(\mathrm{C_3}\) plants.
Water stress reduces photosynthesis indirectly by causing stomatal closure (limiting \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) entry) and leaf wilting (reducing leaf surface area and metabolic activity).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs light saturation with \(10\%\) of full sunlight, \(\mathrm{C_4}\) \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) saturation with \(360\ \mu\text{L L}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{C_3}\) \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) saturation with beyond \(450\ \mu\text{L L}^{-1}\), and water stress with stomatal closure and leaf wilting.
